doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Singing at 11 for the Licavoli mob at the Chateau La France
summary: Worked with Art Tatum for bootleggers' club, saw shotguns stashed, and was tipped ten dollars.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: That’s a great story. You were playing as a young man, not even in your teens yet or were you in your —
What kind of work were you able to do or allowed to do in the clubs?

Well I worked for the local gangsters, the Licavolian mob ran Ohio and part of Illinois. And the Purple Gang ran southern Michigan and the Detroit area. So Michigan was wet and Ohio was dry. So the Licavolis would run liquor down from Michigan into Ohio, into Toledo. And they had this place called the Chateau La France which was a night club that featured a floor show with Art Tatum and me, and I was 11. And the guys that ran the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

liquor that rode shotgun for the trucks, one Packard convertible and another one in the back, there was two guys in front and two in back with sawed off shotguns. They would drive into the back of the club, and we were not allowed in the front of the club. You know Art Tatum and I could entertain the people but then we had to go back into the kitchen area. And back there it was rougher you know. And beside the door there was a barrel and I wondered, what was that barrel. So these guys would come off a run and they’d drive this car back up and park it under the trees out there, and come in the back door with these big overcoats on and the big Borsalino hats and they’d pull these sawed off shotguns out from their coats and put them in this barrel. And I’m watching this. I couldn’t believe it. It was like watching a Warner Brothers movie.
Here we go, you’re still in a movie.

Well to me everything’s a movie. And I was fascinated, I couldn’t believe it. And they would come by where I was standing and they’d say, “hi, kid,” and they’d rub my head you know, which was so demeaning. Because the actual statement was you can always rub a nigger’s head for luck. That was the prevailing statement. So when they did that I’d get so mad. And then they’d put something in my hand, and then when they went I’d be angry. I’d look in my hand, and there’s ten dollars. That would feed my family of 15 for a week. So I’d get a lot less angry. I became philosophical through going through things like that. I would get angry but then I would say, hey if they didn’t do that, what would you do.
